title: Epilogue — Soft Landings
paragraphs: June in Charlotte arrived like a held breath finally released — heat without Caribbean performance, evenings that smelled like cut grass and asphalt cooling, fireflies practicing small lights in the apartment-complex green as if no one had ever cancelled a wedding.

Maya Delgado was twenty-nine still, bare-handed for months, hair longer than cruise February, reliability no longer her only brand. She came home Thursday with grocery bags and a freckle of sun from a site walkthrough at a clinic renovation, and found Julian Park in her kitchen — his kitchen too, three months into a shared lease that was not a rebound erase but a chosen logistics — burning toast with the concentration of a senior designer confronting a hostile interface.
"I had it," he said, dry, when she laughed.

"You never had it." She set the bags down, whole-face smile easy now in ordinary light, and kissed him like wanting that did not need a ship to authorize itself. His hands at her waist. Familiar. Earned again daily.

Friday evening Sofia Reyes came over with Luca and a bottle of something cold and a face that meant adult sidebar after spaghetti. Luca immediately drafted Julian into block towers. Maya washed a plate and waited. Sofia dried. Sister quiet — not Gloria loud.

"I saw Ethan on the greenway," Sofia said, not unkind. "Near the park path. Alone. Headphones. He looked — okay. Not performing okay. Actually walking like a person who had slept. He nodded when he saw me. Didn't run. Didn't ask about you. That felt like grace."
Maya's hands stilled in the water. Soft landing, reported only. Eyes wet without drama. "Thank you."
Sofia squeezed her wrist. "You're allowed to be glad he's breathing without needing him to narrate it to you. You chose hard and clean. He's rebuilding. Stop casting yourself as permanent damage."

Maya nodded, dried her hands, and went to sit on the floor with Luca and Julian until towers fell and bedtime routines reclaimed her sister. After the door closed, Julian looked at her over leftover blocks.
"Ethan weather. Soft. Via Sofia only." Maya leaned her shoulder into his. "I'm glad. And I'm not going to turn glad into a project."
Saturday morning an email waited in Maya's personal inbox under a subject line that made her snort into coffee:
*From the late lounge — ship still sailing*

Mara Quinn — or Mara's dry ghost via some passenger-relations workaround — keeping the door soft without asking them to walk through it. Body short: a photo from the *Aurora Lyric*'s late lounge, empty stools, one glass left on the bar like a joke about unfinished conversations. Under it: *Tell the designer his tip still funds my patience. Tell your face I saw it laugh once for real. No reunion required. — M*
Maya forwarded it to Julian with no commentary. He replied: *Tip was earned. Door stays soft.* Soft hooks unresolved on purpose — Mara, Theo, the ship as postcard, not unfinished novel.

Later, in ordinary kitchen light, Julian dried a plate while Maya answered a work email that had nothing to do with altars. The ring on her right hand now was small and chosen, not a countdown. When they named capacity, it meant room for bad days without disappearing — held in the way he waited for her sentence to finish, and in the way she stopped managing his silence into a problem.

Gloria had planted a white flag of sorts at Sunday dinner: a quiet *I want you happy even when I don't understand the map*, Rafael's tomatoes passed like peace. The cancelled Saturday of March 6 lived in memory as weather metabolized, not as a shrine.
Outside, Charlotte June hummed. Inside, no itinerary owned them. Maya leaned her shoulder into Julian's and let the quiet be enough — stable joy, land-earned, unfinished in the way living things are.
